newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine to launch space satellite from jet by 2005.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine to launch space satellite from jet by 2005.

text.p: Ukraine, forced to rely on Russian cosmodromes for space launches, is working on a project to blast light satellites into orbit from its giant Ruslan aircraft by 2005, a top aviation official said on Wednesday.

Oleh Bohdanov, Deputy Chief Designer of the Kiev-based Antonov planemaker, said designers at the company were planning to launch satellites weighing up to one tonne from its Antonov-124 -- one of the world's biggest planes.
"We are working very hard and it's very realistic to launch light boosters from a plane," Bohdanov told Reuters. "In eight years we will start commercial launches from Ruslan jets."

An AN-124-100 Ruslan jet, weighing 400 tonnes, can carry 150 tonnes for 16,000 km (9,700 miles) non-stop without refuelling. Ruslan has the world record for long-haul flights, staying in the air for more than 24 hours.
The jet flies up to 10 km (six miles) high, meaning the first tough few kilometres after launch would be avoided.

"We would very much welcome foreign investors. We would offer them a share in future profits from commercial launches," Bohdanov said, adding that the Antonov design bureau and Ukraine's National Space Agency had been sponsoring the work themselves.
He declined to say how much cash was needed, but the Den daily said the project, called Oril, cost $70 million and Kiev had already footed half the bill.
The project is targeted at the light end of the satellite launch market which take up about four-fifths of space launches.

Ukraine is already participating in the "Sea Launch" project with U.S. Boeing Co, Norway's Kvaerner and Russia to make 60 commercial launches by the year 2010 from a former oil-extracting sea platform, which would be based near Hawaii.
Ukraine, which has a 15 percent share in the $600 million project, will supply Zenit boosters from its Yuzhmash plant --- once run by President Leonid Kuchma -- in the eastern city of Dnipropetrovsk.

Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said in Kiev last week that Ukraine could help finance Kazakhstan's Baikonur launch site which is run by Russia under a leasing agreement at a cost of $116 million a year.
"Launches from a jet will cost two or three times less than the regular ones," Den wrote.
"But the main thing is that the project gives Ukraine, which has no cosmodrome of its own, a good chance of entering the 21st century with a highly-developed space industry."
